title: Paul Graham on how YC grew by word of mouth, demo day "vertebrae" pitches, and AI's limits
summary: Paul Graham reminisces with Jessica Livingston and Carolyn Levy about how Y Combinator grew with no deliberate marketing: alumni told their friends. He also explains how he coached demo day pitches, expanded founders' ideas, and why founder needs remain the best source of startup ideas even with AI.

principles.text: Growth came from being genuinely helpful so users told their peers; word of mouth compounds exponentially.
principles.quote: I think it was simply that it helped them a lot and they would tell their friends and then their friends would do it, too. And then, you know, well, that's a recipe for exponential growth

principles.text: Publicity only matters if your actual target audience sees it; press the audience doesn't read barely helps.
principles.quote: the only kind of out there that you care about is whether potential applicants know about you.

principles.text: Build a pitch around about five memorable sentences, framed as a logical proof that expected value is high.
principles.quote: you really can only hope that they'll remember about five sentences worth of stuff in the very best case. And so, you should decide in advance what those sentences will be.

principles.text: Pitches should be logical proofs, not fast-talking marketing speak.
principles.quote: Demo day presentation shouldn't be like fast-talking marketing speak. They should be almost like logical proofs of why this company is good to invest in.

principles.text: Early in a startup, often the best help is making the idea much bigger.
principles.quote: I would do it like maybe 1/3 of the office hours I did. We would figure out how to make an idea much bigger.

principles.text: The best source of startup ideas is the founders' own needs, which AI lacks.
principles.quote: You know what the best source of startup ideas is? Your own needs.
